Findings

  • Warmer, mostly in winter. Median winter (DJF) change is — (2030) and — (2035); summer (JJA) moves — and —. California is cooler than 2018 in both projection years, as are SERC in 2030 and ERCOT in 2035 by a small margin.
  • The cold tail moves most, so the distribution narrows. P01 changes by — to — across regions in 2030 (2035: — to —), while P99 shifts — to — (2035: — to —). The P01 to P99 spread narrows in — regions in 2030 and — in 2035.
  • Heating degree days fall, cooling degree days split. HDD changes by — to — in 2030 and — to — in 2035. CDD is above 2018 in — regions in 2030 but — in 2035, with the largest increases in New England, PJM and MISO.
  • Frost hours drop. Hours at or below 0 °C fall by a median — (2030) and — (2035). WECC in 2035 is the one case with more hours below -10 °C than 2018, from a cold late-November spell.
  • Daily temperature range is stable. The mean daily max minus min changes by — to — (2030) and — to — (2035).
  • Single-year deltas mix trend and weather. 2018 had an early January cold wave, the coldest April in more than 20 years and the warmest May on record in the contiguous US (NOAA, see notes). Monthly deltas swing both ways by several degrees, and some regions cool from 2030 to 2035, so part of every difference here is weather, not the SSP2-4.5 trend.

Method and caveats

  • Inputs. 2018: hourly region temperatures for the nine regions (CSV, UTC). Projections: SSP2-4.5 hourly region averages for 2030 and 2035 (workbook dated 2026-10-14, one sheet per region, averaged over the grid points listed in the sheet). Region names match one to one.
  • Time. Both files are in UTC: the afternoon peak falls at 20 to 23 UTC in both. Hours are shifted to local standard time with fixed offsets (California UTC-8, WECC UTC-7, ERCOT, SPP and MISO UTC-6, SERC, PJM, New York and New England UTC-5); the few hours shifted past year end wrap within the same year.
  • Degree days. Daily mean of 24 local hours against 18.3 °C (65 °F), the NOAA convention. Percentiles use all 8,760 hours.
  • One year each. Each column is a single weather year. 2018 had an early January cold wave, the coldest April in more than 20 years and the warmest May on record for the contiguous US. Those months drive the largest monthly deltas. Day-to-day anomalies of the three years are uncorrelated, so the projections are independent model years, not 2018 shifted by a delta.
  • Hourly detail. Both files are hourly. In the projections the average hour-to-hour change rises and falls gradually through the day. In 2018 it alternates at the same UTC hours every day: a near-flat hour, then a jump of about twice the usual size. That looks like data built from a coarser or uneven native time step, or from merged sources, so hourly ramps and the exact diurnal shape compare less well than daily and monthly values.
  • Lower variability in the projections. Standard deviation and day-to-day change are lower in most projection runs. This can be climate signal, a property of the model, or chance; one year per case cannot tell them apart. For load or adequacy work, a multi-year historical baseline and several projection years would separate trend from weather.
